chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
For FY2025, Applied Optoelectronics reported revenue of $455.7M — up 82.8% from $249.4M in FY2024 — on GAAP gross margin of 30.0%, improved from 24.8% the prior year. The result was simultaneously two things: the payoff from a CATV infrastructure upgrade cycle that had been building since 2023, and an accelerating 800G datacenter ramp that, by the fourth quarter, overtook cable as the company's largest revenue line. In Q4 2025, datacenter revenue reached $74.9M against CATV's $54.0M — the first time in the company's 28-year history that the internet data-center segment led the quarterly mix.

## Company in Brief

Applied Optoelectronics — ticker AAOI on the NASDAQ — is headquartered in Sugar Land, Texas, seventeen miles southwest of Houston. It was incorporated on 28 February 1997 by Dr. Chih-Hsiang "Thompson" Lin, who has served as Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer without interruption since inception. At 31 December 2025 the company employed 4,691 people: 548 in the United States, 1,262 in Taiwan, and 2,881 in China. The stock has traded in a five-year range of $1.50 to $223.10, and at the snapshot date of 23 May 2026 stood at approximately $181.

AAOI is a vertically-integrated optical components and transceivers maker: it fabricates its own InP and GaAs laser dies using in-house molecular beam epitaxy and metal-organic chemical vapour deposition processes, then assembles transceivers — including 800G OSFP DR8 and, in volume production since early 2026, 1.6T units — alongside HFC networking equipment, across facilities in Sugar Land, Taipei, and Ningbo. That end-to-end stack, from semiconductor substrate to finished transceiver, distinguishes AAOI structurally from pure-play module assemblers such as Innolight and Eoptolink, which procure laser components externally.

## The FY2025 Revenue Structure

The 82.8% revenue increase in FY2025 was not driven by a single cycle. CATV — principally equipment sold into cable operators' DOCSIS 3.1 and 4.0 network upgrades — accounted for 53.8% of full-year revenue, approximately $245M. The internet data-center segment, carrying 800G transceiver shipments to hyperscale customers, contributed 42.9%, approximately $196M. The quarterly trajectory maps the inflection: total revenue ran at $99.9M in Q1 2025, $103.0M in Q2, $118.6M in Q3, and $134.3M in Q4.

Customer concentration at those revenue levels is severe. [The company's FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm) discloses that Digicomm International — the distribution channel partner through which AAOI sells into the CATV market — represented 53.1% of FY2025 revenue, up from 34.1% in FY2024 and 11.3% in FY2023. Microsoft, the primary hyperscale datacenter customer through FY2025, contributed 28.8%, down from 43.7% in FY2024 as total company revenue expanded faster than that one relationship. Combined, the two customers represented 81.9% of FY2025 revenue.

## The Amazon Variable

In March 2025 AAOI granted Amazon a stock purchase warrant covering up to 7.945M shares, with vesting contingent on cumulative purchase-volume thresholds. Amazon is widely understood — though not named in the filings — to be the hyperscale customer behind a sequence of large orders announced between mid-March and early April 2026: $53M for 800G transceivers, a first-generation $200M-plus commitment for 1.6T transceivers, and a further $71M 800G follow-on, totalling more than $324M from a single buyer across approximately three weeks. If the relationship matures at the scale the order cadence implies, Microsoft's share of the mix will compress further, and a new customer-concentration dynamic — one anchored in the 1.6T generation rather than 800G — will define FY2026 and beyond. The warrant structure means Amazon holds a contingent equity stake whose dilutive weight rises precisely as the commercial relationship deepens; upside that accrues to AAOI shareholders is partially offset by an instrument that transfers value back to the customer as purchase volumes grow.

## The Unresolved Tension

FY2025 is the strongest year in the company's history. Net loss narrowed to $38.2M from $186.7M in FY2024, and GAAP gross margin expanded 520 basis points. By year-end, AAOI was targeting capacity of more than 500,000 transceiver units per month across 800G and 1.6T combined by the close of 2026.

And yet the accumulated deficit on the balance sheet stands at $493.1M — the arithmetic residue of a 2018-to-2023 trough that required multiple dilutive equity raises to survive and has not yet been absorbed by operating profits. The stock's recovery from $1.50 to approximately $181 over five years, roughly a 120-fold move, reflects the market's conviction that what comes next is a sustained operating-leverage cycle rather than a cyclical mean-reversion. Whether that conviction survives the concentration risk embedded in an 81.9% two-customer revenue base — and whether the Amazon warrant redistributes a portion of the upside toward the buyer rather than the seller — is the central question this report exists to answer.

chapters.title: The 28-year founder-led arc
chapters.body:
## The Sugar Land Laboratory, 1997

On February 28, 1997, Dr. Chih-Hsiang Lin — known universally in the optical industry as Thompson — incorporated Applied Optoelectronics in Sugar Land, Texas, a suburban city southwest of Houston whose principal claim to industry at the time was the petrochemical plants lining the Ship Channel. Lin had spent the previous three years as a senior research scientist at the University of Houston, working on laser-diode physics after completing his doctoral work in electrical and computer engineering at the University of Missouri-Columbia, which had followed an undergraduate degree in nuclear engineering at National Tsing Hua University in Taiwan. He was, in the idiom of the industry, a materials scientist who understood how to make light do work at the device level — a relatively rare combination in 1997 that would become a structural competitive advantage two decades later.

The company he founded was small and technically focused: building InP and GaAs laser-diode components for the cable-television and fibre-optic markets using molecular beam epitaxy and metal-organic chemical vapour deposition processes that Lin had been refining since his Missouri years. The premise was vertical integration from the semiconductor wafer outward — a capital-intensive posture that most startups of that era chose not to adopt, preferring to buy laser chips from the merchant market and focus on higher-level assembly. Lin chose the harder path, and that choice became the only reason AAOI survived what came later.

## Building the Stack (1997–2013)

Through the 2000s, the company layered its manufacturing geography carefully. Sugar Land anchored the US operation. Taipei was added for wafer fabrication and module assembly, exploiting Taiwan's deep optoelectronics supply chain. Ningbo, in eastern China, came later for laser-device fabrication and high-volume transceiver assembly at a cost structure that the US facility could not match. By the time of the IPO the company operated three distinct manufacturing nodes across two continents — a supply-chain architecture that looked like overhead in benign markets and a resilience asset in constrained ones.

The revenue base in this period was divided among three markets: cable broadband for the HFC / CATV industry, fibre-to-the-home lasers and transceivers for the telecom sector, and early-generation datacenter optical transceivers. None of these were fast-growing businesses in the pre-2013 period; AAOI was a profitable-ish specialty manufacturer with no obvious reason to go public.

## The IPO and the First Hyperscale Cycle (2013–2017)

AAOI completed its NASDAQ IPO in September 2013, pricing in the vicinity of $10 per share — a listing that, in hindsight, arrived at almost exactly the moment the hyperscale datacenter capex cycle was preparing to absorb optical transceivers at a scale the industry had not previously contemplated. [S-1 prospectus, September 2013]

The first major cyclical lift arrived between 2015 and 2017 with the 100G datacenter transceiver ramp at Microsoft and Amazon. The numbers were abrupt. Revenue accelerated through the mid-teens to a peak of $382 million in FY2017, and the stock — which had spent its first years trading between $5 and $20 — reached approximately $96 in mid-2017, implying a market capitalisation that reflected an emerging consensus that AAOI had found a structural role in the hyperscale supply chain rather than merely a transient product win. The vertical integration that Lin had insisted upon from the start gave the company a gross-margin structure that pure-play transceiver assemblers could not match when demand exceeded supply.

This was AAOI's first full encounter with the dynamic that has defined its operating model ever since: a single hyperscaler product-generation transition can multiply revenue in eighteen months or halve it in twelve. The lesson embedded itself early.

## The Long Trough (2018–2023)

From 2018 the company entered what its own filings would eventually characterise, in the aggregate, as a period of sustained operational difficulty. Microsoft's hyperscale buying pattern shifted toward alternative suppliers; Amazon's purchasing volume through AAOI declined from its 100G peak; the cable MSO capex cycle turned weak as operators deferred HFC upgrade spending; and the 400G transceiver ramp that was supposed to replace the 100G volumes was repeatedly delayed by qualification slips that added quarters to the engineering timeline. Revenue fell from $382 million in 2017 to approximately $187 million in 2023, and the gross-margin structure that had looked like a moat in 2017 became a liability as fixed costs for the Texas, Taiwan, and Ningbo facilities ran against a revenue base that had contracted by more than half.

The stock reflected this with a severity that few US-listed semiconductor names have survived. From the $96 peak in mid-2017, AAOI's share price fell to approximately $1.50 in 2023 — a decline of more than 98%. The company conducted multiple equity raises through the trough to sustain liquidity, diluting shareholders and accumulating a deficit that reached $493.1 million by the end of FY2025. [FY2025 10-K, SEC filing]

What makes the trough notable in a governance context is what did not happen: Thompson Lin did not leave. He remained Chairman, President, and Chief Executive throughout the six-year contraction — an unusual continuity for a US-listed company under that kind of shareholder pressure. The board did not install an operational turnaround specialist or a private-equity-style restructuring executive. Lin, who had founded the company at the component level, ran it through the worst years of its history with the same vertically integrated operating model he had built in 1997.

## Two Engines Fire Simultaneously (2024–2025)

The recovery that began in 2024 was structurally unusual. Most cyclical optical-component companies have one demand engine: either the hyperscale datacenter cycle or the cable broadband upgrade cycle. AAOI had both turn positive in the same fiscal year.

The cable-industry recovery was driven by the DOCSIS 4.0 / 1.8 GHz amplifier upgrade cycle, which forced MSOs to commit capex they had deferred through the trough years. The beneficiary inside AAOI's revenue line was Digicomm, the company's principal CATV distribution channel partner, whose share of AAOI's total revenue moved from 11.3% in FY2023 to 34.1% in FY2024 to 53.1% in FY2025. [FY2025 10-K] Simultaneously, the AI infrastructure buildout drove Microsoft and Amazon back into urgent 800G optical transceiver procurement — and AAOI's in-house laser fabrication capability, which had been expensive overhead in a slow market, made it one of a short list of suppliers with both the technical qualification and the manufacturing scale to respond.

The result was FY2025 revenue of $455.7 million, an 82.8% increase over FY2024's $249.4 million, on a GAAP gross margin of 30.0% (up from 24.8%), with a net loss narrowed to $38.2 million from $186.7 million the prior year. [FY2025 Q4 press release; FY2025 10-K]

| Metric | FY2023 (approx.) | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue ($M) | ~187 | 249.4 | 455.7 |
| GAAP gross margin | — | 24.8% | 30.0% |
| Net loss ($M) | — | (186.7) | (38.2) |
| Digicomm % of revenue | 11.3% | 34.1% | 53.1% |
| Microsoft % of revenue | ~46.6% | 43.7% | 28.8% |

The quarterly inflection was sharpest in Q4 2025, when datacenter revenue reached $74.9 million against CATV revenue of $54.0 million — the first quarter in the company's history that the datacenter segment exceeded cable. The mix that had defined AAOI since the 1990s was, for the first time, inverting.

## The Amazon Warrant and the 1.6T Era

In March 2025, AAOI filed an 8-K disclosing that it had granted Amazon a stock purchase warrant for up to 7.945 million shares, structured as a volume-vesting instrument — meaning Amazon earns warrant tranches against purchase thresholds rather than on a time schedule. [Amazon warrant 8-K, March 2025] The warrant's existence confirmed a deepening supply relationship that the formal 10-K customer disclosures had not yet captured: Amazon did not appear as a greater-than-10% customer in the FY2025 annual filing, a recognition lag that reflects purchase-cycle timing rather than any absence of commercial engagement.

Between March and early April 2026, AAOI announced a sequence of orders from what it described as "one major hyperscale customer" — widely understood by sell-side analysts to be Amazon — that totalled more than $324 million in aggregate: an initial $53 million for 800G transceivers in March, followed by a purchase order exceeding $200 million for 1.6T transceivers representing first-volume production, and an additional $71 million 800G order in early April. [March 2026 and April 2026 hyperscaler order announcements] The 1.6T order is the commercially significant one: it positions AAOI as among the first optical transceiver suppliers with qualified product at the line rate above 800G, a generation transition that the broader market expects to govern AI datacenter optics through at least 2027. The company had guided toward 500,000 or more combined 800G and 1.6T units per month in manufacturing capacity by the end of FY2026.

## Twenty-Eight Years, One Name on the Door

The equity story at the May 2026 snapshot is not separable from Lin's continuity. Applied Optoelectronics went through a period between 2018 and 2023 that would have, in most governance frameworks, produced a CEO change and possibly a strategic transaction — a sale to a larger optics player, a privatisation, or a recapitalisation that transferred control. None of that happened. The company emerged from the trough with its vertical integration intact, its manufacturing footprint across three geographies operational, and its founder still running it.

The stock moved from $1.50 to approximately $181 over the five years through the snapshot date — a roughly 120-fold appreciation that simultaneously reflected the CATV cyclical recovery, the AI-optics ramp, and the option value of being one of a small handful of vertically integrated optical transceiver suppliers qualified at 800G and entering qualification at 1.6T. The accumulated deficit of $493.1 million and the 81.9% combined customer concentration in Digicomm and Microsoft remain the structural caution flags. But $324 million in near-term orders from a single hyperscaler, a warrant that aligns Amazon's interests with AAOI's equity price, and a gross-margin structure finally recovering toward the levels the company last saw at the 2017 peak suggest that the 28 years of vertical-integration investment Lin refused to abandon through the worst of the cycle may be the foundation for a genuinely different second act — not a turnaround imposed from outside, but the original strategy, finally meeting the market it was built for.

chapters.title: Three businesses, one cycle each
chapters.body:
## A company with three clocks

Applied Optoelectronics reported $455.7 million in revenue for fiscal 2025, an 82.8 percent increase over the prior year that the company described as its strongest annual result in 28 years of existence. The number is real, but it obscures something more interesting: it was produced by three separate product franchises running on entirely different business cycles, only two of which were meaningfully contributing, and only one of which was genuinely accelerating by year-end.

Understanding AAOI at the FY2025 snapshot requires holding those three clocks simultaneously.

## CATV: the revenue engine that rebuilt the balance sheet

The cable television segment — HFC amplifiers, the Quantum18 1.8-GHz node platform, and the QuantumLink management software layer — accounted for 53.8 percent of FY2025 revenue, approximately $245.2 million, per the company's [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm). It was the segment that rescued the company's income statement.

The structural driver is the DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle. US cable operators — Comcast, Charter, Cox — are mid-decade through a multi-billion-dollar plant modernisation that requires replacing legacy HFC amplifiers with 1.8-GHz-capable hardware. AAOI's Quantum18 product line is qualified for that architecture, and the company sells into that channel exclusively through Digicomm International, a privately-held US broadband equipment distributor acquired by The Beekman Group in 2018. Digicomm's share of AAOI revenue went from 11.3 percent in FY2023 to 34.1 percent in FY2024 to 53.1 percent in FY2025, representing an estimated $242 million — essentially the entire CATV segment flowing through a single channel partner.

That concentration is both a structural vulnerability and, for now, a sign of how thoroughly AAOI dominates its niche. The cable operators are not yet done spending. The DOCSIS 4.0 plant refresh is a multi-year programme, and AAOI's Q3 2025 CATV result — $70.6 million, a record, more than three times the prior-year quarter and 26 percent ahead of Q2 2025 — made clear that the cycle had not peaked at mid-year. The sequential moderation to $54.0 million in Q4 2025 was read by the company as normal programme cadence rather than demand deterioration.

## Internet Data Center: the line-rate ladder

The datacenter segment generated approximately $195.5 million in FY2025, representing 42.9 percent of revenue. That figure, and the trajectory embedded within it, is the more consequential story for investors thinking about FY2026 and beyond.

AAOI's transceiver line spans four active generations, and the economics and volumes of each tell a different story in FY2025.

| Generation | FY2025 directional trend | Q3 2025 YoY | Strategic position |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100G | Low-margin, declining ASP; still volume-relevant | +32% YoY | Harvested; Microsoft legacy |
| 400G | Being skipped by leading AI-workload operators | –65% YoY; $7.1M in Q3 | Structurally adverse |
| 800G (OSFP DR8) | Volume ramp through FY2025; principal margin driver | Ramping | Qualified at Microsoft and Amazon |
| 1.6T | First volume order March 2026, $200M | Pre-revenue at snapshot | Next-cycle anchor |

The 400G data point requires emphasis. In Q3 2025, that generation produced only $7.1 million of revenue — a 65 percent year-on-year decline — against a 100G line that was simultaneously up 32 percent, per the [Q3 2025 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000168316825008029/aaoi_ex9901.htm). The reason is architectural: leading AI-infrastructure operators, building out large-scale GPU clusters in 2024 and 2025, moved directly from 100G back-plane designs to 800G interconnect, compressing or eliminating the 400G buildout cycle that an earlier forecast vintage would have projected. For AAOI, this was strategically positive — the company had qualified its 800G OSFP DR8 transceiver with both Microsoft and the counterparty associated with the March 2025 Amazon warrant before 400G demand peaked, meaning it was not caught holding inventory or committed capacity in a generation the market was bypassing.

The 800G ramp was the dominant margin event of FY2025. AAOI's gross margin expanded from 24.8 percent in FY2024 to 30.0 percent in FY2025, a 520-basis-point improvement driven primarily by the higher average selling prices of 800G units relative to 100G, and by the operating leverage embedded in the company's vertically-integrated cost structure. Microsoft has been the anchor datacenter customer through this cycle, representing 28.8 percent of FY2025 revenue — still the single largest hyperscale relationship in absolute dollars, even as its percentage share declined from 43.7 percent in FY2024 as total revenue grew.

## Telecom and FTTH: the vestigial tail

The third segment, combining telecom and FTTH, contributed a combined 3.3 percent of FY2025 revenue — approximately $15.1 million — and requires little analytical attention except as a reminder of what AAOI once was. The company built much of its original revenue on FTTH components during the fiber-to-the-home buildouts of the early 2010s, and the telecom line was substantively larger in prior cycles. At $13.7 million (telecom) and $1.4 million (FTTH and other), these segments are now niche applications running on legacy programme spending, not growth contributors. They are retained because the product families share manufacturing infrastructure with the other segments, not because they represent independent commercial opportunity.

## Vertical integration as a cost-structure argument

The phrase "vertically integrated" carries different weight depending on what a company actually owns. For AAOI, the claim rests on something specific: the company fabricates its own indium phosphide and gallium arsenide laser dies using molecular beam epitaxy and metal-organic chemical vapour deposition processes in-house, at its Sugar Land and Ningbo facilities. At the scale AAOI operates — roughly 4,700 employees, 199 US-issued patents, R&D staff that includes 14 PhD-level researchers — this is not unusual by the standards of Coherent or Lumentum, but it is unusual for a company at AAOI's revenue tier.

The business consequence is gross-margin stability relative to module-assembler peers. Companies such as Innolight and Eoptolink — the dominant Chinese transceiver assemblers by volume — source laser dies from external wafer suppliers and build margin on throughput efficiency and component procurement skill. When upstream laser-die pricing rises, or when DSP silicon from Marvell or Broadcom commands premium lead times, assemblers feel the squeeze immediately. AAOI's internal laser fabrication effectively fixes a portion of its cost-of-goods at its own loaded manufacturing cost rather than the spot market, and the gap between those two figures widens during periods of supply tightness — precisely when hyperscalers are placing large, urgent orders.

The remaining external dependencies — OSFP cages and connectors from TE Connectivity and Amphenol, clock-data-recovery DSPs, optical isolators — are real, but they represent the commoditised layers of the bill of materials rather than the differentiated components. The 35 percent of exit-FY2025 800G capacity that AAOI operates from Sugar Land is a secondary structural argument: a US-domiciled supply of transceiver production that hyperscalers treating supply-chain resilience as a procurement criterion value separately from pure unit economics.

## Q3 2025: the mixed-signal quarter

The Q3 2025 result — $118.6 million in total revenue, with a 28.0 percent GAAP gross margin — served as an unintentional stress test of the segment thesis. CATV hit a record $70.6 million; the datacenter segment came in at $43.9 million, up 7 percent year-on-year but down sequentially. Within that datacenter number, 100G was solid, 400G had collapsed, and 800G had not yet fully absorbed the demand that would arrive in Q4.

The quarter demonstrated both the insulation that CATV provides — the segment's strength kept consolidated revenue growing even as datacenter temporarily softened — and the internal imbalance in the datacenter product mix. An analyst reading only the datacenter headline might have concluded the AI-optics narrative was stalling. An analyst decomposing the generation-level detail would have recognised that the 400G decline was structural exit, not demand destruction, and that 800G was the relevant signal.

## Q4 2025: the inversion

The Q4 2025 report, published in early 2026, produced the number that reframed the narrative. Datacenter revenue reached $74.9 million; CATV came in at $54.0 million. It was the first quarter in AAOI's history where its datacenter segment exceeded its cable segment, according to the [Q4 and FY2025 earnings release](https://investors.ao-inc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-optoelectronics-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-5).

The framing matters: this inversion happened against a CATV segment that was not falling. The $54.0 million CATV quarter was consistent with a healthy programme cadence; it was not a business under pressure. The inflection came from datacenter accelerating, not from cable deteriorating. That distinction is important for reading forward — it suggests the two engines are not cannibalising each other's resources, that AAOI's manufacturing infrastructure was scaling to serve both simultaneously.

## A business in transition, measured by a year

At the fiscal-year level, AAOI in 2025 looked like a nearly 50-50 CATV-datacenter business: $245.2 million in cable, $195.5 million in datacenter. At the quarterly level, by year-end, it looked like a company transitioning into a majority-datacenter franchise for the first time since its 2017 peak. The order book announced in March and April 2026 — $53 million in 800G, then a $200 million first-volume 1.6T order, then an additional $71 million in 800G, all from one hyperscale customer in a six-week span, totalling more than $324 million — is the leading indicator that makes the trajectory legible.

The [Lightreading report on the 1.6T order](https://www.lightreading.com/ai-machine-learning/aoi-receives-first-volume-order-of-1-6t-data-center-transceivers-from-major-hyperscale-customer) described it as the first volume commercial order AAOI had received for that generation. Whether that hyperscale customer is Amazon — the warrant holder since March 2025, with up to 7.945 million shares contingent on purchase volumes — or another party, the size and timing signal that the next cycle layer is not a roadmap promise. It is an active customer programme. By FY2026, absent a material demand reversal, AAOI will almost certainly be a majority-datacenter company by annual revenue for the first time in nearly a decade. That structural shift, from cable-dominant to datacenter-dominant, is what the three-segment architecture has been quietly assembling since 2023.

chapters.title: Inside the operating leverage
chapters.body:
## The numbers that ended the trough

For six consecutive quarters beginning in Q3 2024, Applied Optoelectronics reported sequential revenue growth — a streak that, by the company's own history, was without precedent. The progression was deliberate in its geometry: Q3 2024 delivered $65.2 million; Q4 2024 broke $100 million for the first time at $100.3 million; and the line continued through Q1 2025 ($99.9 million), Q2 2025 ($103.0 million), Q3 2025 ($118.6 million), and Q4 2025 ($134.3 million). By the time the full-year 2025 result was reported — $455.7 million, up 82.8 percent year-on-year — the company had nearly doubled in a single calendar year. [FY2025 Q4 press release](https://investors.ao-inc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-optoelectronics-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-5)

That aggregate, however, obscures what made the FY2025 result structurally interesting rather than merely large. Revenue growth at this rate can be an accounting event — volume times price, concentrated in a fortunate product cycle — or it can represent a genuine change in unit economics. The evidence from the margin line argues for the latter, though with caveats the balance sheet imposes honestly.

## Gross margin as the operative signal

AAOI's GAAP gross margin in FY2025 reached 30.0 percent, up 520 basis points from the 24.8 percent reported in FY2024. At revenue nearly double the prior year, that improvement compounds: the company earned roughly $136.7 million in gross profit in 2025 against approximately $61.9 million in 2024 — a 121 percent increase in gross dollars on 83 percent more revenue. [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm) That differential is the definition of operating leverage beginning to assert itself.

The quarterly granularity adds texture. Q3 2025 GAAP gross margin came in at 28.0 percent — below the full-year average, reflecting the period when CATV still dominated the mix. The non-GAAP figure for the same quarter, stripping out stock-based compensation and certain non-cash items, was 31.0 percent. [Q3 2025 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774925033627/aaoi20250930_10q.htm) The 300-basis-point gap between GAAP and non-GAAP is itself a data point: it reflects the equity-heavy compensation structure the company deployed during its trough years to retain engineers when cash was constrained. As that legacy dilution flows through the income statement, it will compress — but until then, investors watching the GAAP line are paying a partial toll on the recovery.

The comparison to sector peers is instructive and honest. At 30 percent GAAP gross margin, AAOI sits below where Lumentum has historically operated — roughly 35 to 37 percent through its own datacenter product cycles — and a wider gap below Coherent, which has reported margins in the high thirties. The distance is partly explainable by product mix (the CATV channel runs leaner than pure datacenter transceivers) and partly by scale. At roughly 100,000 units per month of 800G production capacity at year-end 2025, with 35 percent of that running in Sugar Land, the company was not yet operating at the volumes where fixed manufacturing overhead spreads most favourably. [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm) The 1.6T ramp — and the 500,000-plus combined units-per-month target the company set for end of 2026 — is where the next tranche of margin compression could theoretically materialise. Whether it does depends on pricing discipline in a market where multiple vendors are racing for the same hyperscaler purchase orders.

## Revenue did not buy opex

The operating expense story is, in its own right, a structural proof point. Revenue grew 83 percent in FY2025; the company did not double its operating cost base to generate it.

In FY2024, with $249.4 million in revenue and a net loss of $186.7 million, the SG&A and R&D burden — as a share of the revenue line — was structurally punitive. Fixed costs appropriate for a $400 million business (the pre-trough peak) were being spread across a sub-$250 million revenue line. Engineering headcount required to maintain a full vertical stack — the company employed 4,691 people by December 2025, including 425 dedicated to R&D — does not compress easily when order volumes fall. [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm) The result was a cost structure with nowhere to hide.

The FY2025 net loss of $38.2 million, against $186.7 million in FY2024, represents a $148.5 million swing. Some portion of that improvement is genuine margin expansion — real absorption of fixed manufacturing costs as volumes rose. Some portion is simply coverage of previously uncovered overhead. The two are difficult to decompose from outside the company, but the directionality is unambiguous: revenue scale covered costs already in place, rather than revenue growth demanding proportional new cost investment. That is the mechanism of operating leverage.

What the FY2025 result does not yet show is operating income turning positive. The remaining $38.2 million net loss means that at $455.7 million in revenue and 30 percent gross margins, AAOI had not crossed the breakeven threshold. R&D investment critical for the 1.6T product transition and capital expenditure tied to the capacity expansion explain part of the gap. So does the non-cash equity compensation working through the P&L. No claim of imminent GAAP profitability would be credible against that backdrop.

## The weight of the deficit

The accumulated deficit of $493.1 million on the FY2025 balance sheet is not a one-year artifact. [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm) It was assembled across roughly half a decade of impairments, inventory write-downs, and equity-funded operating losses that ran from approximately 2018 through 2023 — years when CATV capital spending collapsed, datacenter customers consolidated their supplier rosters, and AAOI's revenue fell from its peak above $400 million toward a trough that required emergency capital raises and sustained dilution to survive. The company is firmly on the other side of that trough. The balance sheet still carries the mark.

To invert $493.1 million in accumulated deficit at current loss levels would require, arithmetically, more years of net income than the company has existed as a public company. The path to positive retained earnings runs through sustained profitability at margins meaningfully above where the company stands today. That is not a dismissal of the progress; it is a framing of how much distance remains between "best year in company history" and "financially normalised franchise."

## Two customers, one story

| Customer | FY2023 Share | FY2024 Share | FY2025 Share | FY2025 Implied Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Digicomm | 11.3% | 34.1% | 53.1% | ~$242M |
| Microsoft | 46.6% | 43.7% | 28.8% | ~$131M |
| **Combined** | **57.9%** | **77.8%** | **81.9%** | **~$373M** |
| All others | 42.1% | 22.2% | 18.1% | ~$83M |

*Source: [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm)*

In plain terms: $373 million of FY2025 revenue came from two customers. The remaining $83 million — every other distributor, telecom operator, and integrator that engaged AAOI commercially in calendar 2025 — was itself larger than total company revenue in FY2023. The "other" bucket is not small in absolute terms. But at the snapshot date, AAOI had, in effect, two customers above any threshold of materiality.

Digicomm's trajectory is the more dramatic. From 11.3 percent of revenue in FY2023 to 53.1 percent in FY2025, it tripled its share in two years. Digicomm is the channel partner for the CATV recovery — the conduit through which US cable operators, rebuilding and upgrading their plant, placed orders for AAOI's CATV transceivers. The CATV segment contributed 53.8 percent of FY2025 revenue, roughly $245 million, and Digicomm's concentration tracks directly. The relationship is not incidental to the FY2025 result; it is the majority of it.

Microsoft's share fell from 43.7 percent in FY2024 to 28.8 percent in FY2025 — not because the absolute dollar relationship weakened, but because Digicomm's surge expanded the denominator. The implied $131 million from Microsoft in FY2025 compares to roughly $109 million implied from the prior year's base — a growing absolute relationship. What changed is the portfolio weight, and the optics of dependence. Crucially, Q4 2025 marked the first quarter in which datacenter revenue — $74.9 million — exceeded CATV at $54.0 million, a crossover that illustrated the emerging mix shift beneath the headline concentration numbers. [FY2025 Q4 press release](https://investors.ao-inc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-optoelectronics-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-5)

The arrival of the Amazon warrant in March 2025 — 7,945,000 shares subject to vesting against purchase volume thresholds — was the first explicit signal that AAOI was building a third hyperscaler anchor into its customer base. [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm) The order announcements that followed in early 2026 — a $53 million 800G tranche, then a $200 million 1.6T initial order, then $71 million in additional 800G, for a combined $324 million from one hyperscale customer — began converting that signal into revenue backlog. Should those orders flow through as reported, the FY2026 customer concentration table will look materially different: Digicomm's CATV share declining as a proportion, Microsoft holding, and a third major hyperscaler entering the top line at meaningful scale.

## Capex as the cost of the next margin tier

The operating leverage of FY2025 did not produce free cash flow that the company redeployed against its accumulated deficit. It could not. Capital expenditures tied to the capacity expansion — from roughly 100,000 units per month of 800G at year-end 2025, 35 percent of which ran through Sugar Land, toward a target exceeding 500,000 combined 800G and 1.6T units per month by end of 2026 — consumed the incremental cash the margin improvement generated. [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm)

This is the correct investment decision given the order environment. The customer order book argues for it. The Amazon relationship argues for it. The competitive positioning in 1.6T — where AAOI's vertical integration from InP wafer through transceiver assembly offers cost and lead-time advantages that fabless competitors cannot replicate — argues for it. But it means that the leverage story visible in FY2025's income statement did not translate into balance sheet repair. The $493.1 million accumulated deficit did not narrow in proportion to the $148.5 million swing in net loss, because the business consumed capital to fund its own next chapter.

That is the structural condition of AAOI at the snapshot date: generating its highest gross profit in company history, spending aggressively to scale into the next product generation, carrying the scar tissue of a five-year trough on its balance sheet, and dependent on two customers for more than four-fifths of its revenue. The FY2025 income statement is the strongest argument for the bull case. The accumulated deficit, the customer concentration table, and the capex programme are the three honest qualifications that sit alongside it.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
Applied Optoelectronics entered 2024 as a speculative micro-cap trading below $2 per share. By the frozen snapshot of May 23, 2026, the stock had reached approximately $181 — a 90-fold appreciation in roughly 28 months that encodes a complete narrative revision. The market ceased pricing a capital-intensive components maker on liquidation value and began pricing it on a multiple befitting a hyperscale-capex beneficiary in a structural AI buildout. The question a valuation chapter has to answer is whether that revision was proportionate, premature, or still incomplete.

## Building the Market Cap

Reasoning from AAOI's last-reported share count — approximately 29–31 million basic shares outstanding as of December 31, 2025, per the [10-K filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm) — a $181 share price implies a basic market capitalisation of roughly $5.3–5.6 billion. The figure is not exact because the company had been issuing equity for capacity investment and the precise end-of-Q1 2026 count is not cited in the prep data; analysts should verify from the most recent 10-Q.

The Amazon warrant is not a footnote. Covering 7.945 million shares with vesting tied to purchase-volume thresholds, it extends the diluted share count to approximately 37–39 million, or a fully diluted market cap of $6.7–7.1 billion at the snapshot price — a 25–26 percent dilution event that sits at the centre of every serious bull-case model. The structural linkage is precise: every dollar of Amazon revenue that vests additional warrant tranches simultaneously creates revenue and destroys per-share value for everyone else on the cap table.

## Current Multiples

On FY2025 revenue of $455.7 million, the implied EV/Sales multiple — using basic market cap and a conservative net-debt estimate, given AAOI was actively financing US manufacturing expansion — falls in the range of 11–13x. That is not a commodity-hardware multiple; it is a mid-tier software multiple applied to an optical-components manufacturer, and it demands justification.

The GAAP P/E ratio is mathematically inapplicable: AAOI reported a net loss of $38.2 million in FY2025, its narrowest since at least FY2018, but a loss nonetheless. Trailing EV/EBITDA suffers the same constraint — depreciation and stock compensation can surface a positive adjusted EBITDA, but the multiple would exceed 100x on a trailing basis and is not analytically useful. The operative multiples therefore anchor on forward revenue and gross profit, where the $324 million-plus in orders placed by one hyperscale customer in March–April 2026 provides an unusually concrete near-term floor. If that order book flows through in FY2026 alongside a continuation of the CATV channel and the Microsoft relationship, FY2026 revenue is plausibly in the $750–900 million range. At that midpoint, EV/Sales compresses toward 7x forward — still a sector premium, but within reach for a company printing 83 percent revenue growth with margin trajectory positive.

## Historical Multiple Range

The current multiple represents a violent re-rating from the 2018–2023 trough. During the extended CATV down-cycle, AAOI spent long stretches trading below book value — itself depressed by $493.1 million in accumulated losses — and active analysts were deploying distressed-asset frameworks or sum-of-the-parts scenarios anchored to the Taiwan wafer assets. EV/Sales in the 0.3–0.8x range was the norm through much of 2020–2022.

The inflection began with the CATV cyclical recovery in late 2023 and accelerated through 2024 as the Digicomm distribution relationship — 11.3 percent of revenue in FY2023, 34.1 percent in FY2024 — ballooned to 53.1 percent in FY2025, signalling a channel ramp the market began extrapolating toward the datacenter thesis. By the time Q4 2025 datacenter revenue crossed above CATV for the first time ($74.9 million versus $54.0 million per the [Q4 2025 earnings release](https://investors.ao-inc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-optoelectronics-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-5)), the multiple re-rating had already anticipated the handoff. The risk embedded in that history is reversion: AAOI has traded at elevated multiples before — briefly in 2017 when it was still primarily a CATV play — and those multiples compressed toward zero when the cycle turned.

## Peer-Group Comparison

The natural comparison set combines vertically integrated optical component makers, transceiver specialists, and capital-light contract manufacturers. Multiples below are approximate as of the snapshot period.

| Company | Ticker | Model | EV/Sales (TTM) | EV/EBITDA (TTM) | Gross Margin | Rev Growth YoY |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Applied Optoelectronics | AAOI | Integrated transceiver + laser | ~12x | N/M | 30.0% | +82.8% |
| Coherent Corp | COHR | Diversified photonics + datacom | ~4–5x | ~22–25x | ~40–42% | ~+20–25% |
| Lumentum Holdings | LITE | Laser components + 3D sensing | ~4–6x | ~18–22x | ~38–42% | ~+15–20% |
| Fabrinet | FN | Optical contract manufacturing | ~1.5–2x | ~15–18x | ~11–13% | ~+10–15% |
| Ciena Corp | CIEN | Optical networking systems | ~2–3x | ~15–20x | ~46–48% | ~+8–12% |
| Viavi Solutions | VIAV | Network test + optical components | ~2–3x | ~10–14x | ~55–58% | Low single-digit |

*Peer multiples are estimates based on last-available public filings and approximate share prices as of the snapshot window; all should be independently verified.*

AAOI's trailing EV/Sales premium to peers is roughly 2–3x the comparable set. That premium is partially justified by a growth rate no comparable approaches. It is partially undermined by a gross-margin discount: AAOI's 30.0 percent sits well below what Coherent and Lumentum achieve with similar vertical integration, suggesting either a structural pricing concession, a mix effect from high-volume CATV at scale, or simply that the operating leverage cycle is earlier here than anywhere else in the table.

## What the Current Price Implies

A reverse-engineered DCF at $181 on basic shares requires approximately $750 million of FY2026 revenue, gross margin reaching 34–36 percent by FY2027 as 1.6T product mix builds, terminal EBIT margins of 15–18 percent, and a discount rate of 10–12 percent. Those assumptions produce a fair-value range of roughly $160–190 per basic share — which neatly brackets the snapshot price.

The problem is the dilution bridge. Full exercise of the Amazon warrant at sustained FY2026 volumes adds approximately 26 percent to the share count, mechanically reducing per-share intrinsic value by a commensurate amount — all else equal, pushing fair value toward $130–150 on the same model. The market at $181 is therefore pricing either partial warrant exercise or embedding incremental Amazon revenue that offsets the dilution dollar-for-dollar. The distinction matters enormously: if the warrant vests primarily because Amazon is placing $200-million-plus purchase orders, the revenue offsets and the per-share math improves. If warrant vesting accelerates faster than revenue compounds, dilution wins.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $280–320 per share.** FY2026 revenue reaches $850–950 million as AAOI executes the confirmed $324 million-plus order book and capacity ramps to the stated 500,000 units per month target by year-end 2026. Gross margins reach 36–38 percent as 1.6T ASPs lift the blended rate and US automation reduces unit costs. GAAP net income profitability emerges in H2 2026, widening the institutional buyer universe. The Amazon warrant is offset by incremental revenue rather than representing net dilution. Applied multiple: 13–15x EV/Sales on FY2026 forward revenue.

**Base case — $160–200 per share.** FY2026 revenue settles at $700–800 million, consistent with confirmed orders plus moderate continuation of existing channels. Gross margins reach 33–35 percent. Net loss narrows toward breakeven; positive free cash flow begins to emerge. The Amazon warrant vests approximately halfway, adding roughly four million incremental shares. Applied multiple: 9–11x EV/Sales on FY2026 revenue. The stock trades roughly at current levels or a slight discount as the re-rating moderates from its steepest gradient.

**Bear case — $70–90 per share.** Execution slips — shipment timing, component supply, or a pause in hyperscale capex following any macro or regulatory shock. FY2026 revenue falls toward $550–600 million. Gross margins stagnate as CATV pricing concessions limit blended upside. Microsoft's dollar volume declines rather than holding flat, and no third significant customer materialises to reduce concentration risk. The $493.1 million accumulated deficit re-emerges as a balance-sheet narrative if cash burn resumes. Applied multiple: 5–7x EV/Sales on FY2026 forward revenue.

## Gap Between Consensus and This Dossier's Read

The market at $181 is squarely inside the base-to-bull corridor but appears to embed limited credit for the warrant-dilution mechanics. A careful reading of the order structure reveals that Amazon's purchase volumes both trigger revenue recognition and vest the dilutive warrant — meaning every dollar of the most headline-grabbing revenue comes with a fractional share issuance attached. That linkage is systematically underweighted in screens that display EV/Sales without adjusting for contingent dilution.

The second gap is concentration. An 81.9 percent two-customer revenue share is not a condition that growth multiples typically discount until the moment a customer reduces orders — at which point the discount arrives all at once. The Digicomm relationship, which tripled from 11 percent of revenue in FY2023 to 53 percent in FY2025, has no public contractual floor cited in the 10-K.

> "We believe our vertical integration and product breadth will continue to differentiate us in the datacenter market," management stated in the Q4 2025 earnings release.

That may be true. The differentiation is real. But vertical integration, by itself, does not prevent a single large customer from sourcing optionally from a second qualified vendor when lead times compress and pricing competition intensifies. At 12x trailing sales, the stock is priced for the thesis, not for the hedge.

chapters.title: Six quarters of upward sequential
chapters.body:
The numbers run like a metronome — $65.2 million, $100.3 million, $99.9 million, $103.0 million, $118.6 million, $134.3 million — six consecutive quarters of upward sequential revenue from Q3 2024 through Q4 2025. For Applied Optoelectronics, that sequence represents a full-company recovery from what came close to an existential trough. For investors who held through the bottom, it represents a roughly 120x return from the 2023 stock-price low of $1.50. Understanding the chapter requires understanding not only what drove each quarter, but why the market chose to price the recovery in advance of it.

## The trough quarter: Q3 2024

In the summer of 2024, AAOI's revenue trajectory had been negative or flat for the better part of six years. The company had watched its stock fall from a 2017 peak near $96 to the 2023 low, and the $65.2 million Q3 2024 print was, in absolute terms, consistent with the depressed base of the preceding trough years. What the headline number did not yet reflect was that two things were turning simultaneously: the CATV industry's return to amplifier capital expenditure for DOCSIS 4.0 node upgrades, and the early stages of hyperscale datacenter interest in AAOI's next-generation transceiver roadmap.

Gross margin for the quarter came in at 24.4%, still compressed beneath the cost structure of a company carrying manufacturing capacity built for volumes that had not yet materialised. The question for management was whether the CATV orders building in the backlog, and the early 800G datacenter qualification dialogue then underway, would convert fast enough to change the operating-leverage arithmetic before the $493.1 million accumulated deficit became a binding constraint.

## Breaking the threshold: Q4 2024

Q4 2024 answered the first part of that question decisively. Revenue of [$100.3 million](https://investors.ao-inc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-optoelectronics-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-5) was the company's first $100 million-plus quarter in several years, driven — in management's own framing — by a CATV ramp that moved faster than the underlying tone of the order book had implied.

> "We are pleased to have generated a solid quarter, driven by strength in both our datacenter and CATV businesses. We saw a significant increase in our CATV business due to a ramp in orders for our 1.8 GHz amplifier products, which resulted in revenue growth that more than doubled sequentially. During the quarter we also received a substantial order for our Quantum Bandwidth® networking products from a top North American cable operator." — Dr. Chih-Hsiang "Thompson" Lin, President & CEO, [Q4 2024 earnings press release](https://investors.ao-inc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-optoelectronics-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-5), February 26, 2025

The 1.8 GHz amplifier call-out was structurally important. Cable MSOs mid-cycle on DOCSIS 4.0 node splits required amplifiers rated to 1.8 GHz spectrum, and AAOI's vertically integrated laser-fabrication capability in Sugar Land positioned it as one of a small number of qualified suppliers. The distribution of that CATV volume ran almost entirely through Digicomm International, which saw its revenue share rise from 11.3% of AAOI's total in 2023 to 34.1% in FY2024.

CFO Stefan Murry flagged the forward capital investment at the same release, pointing toward a capex cycle that would prove consequential by year-end 2025: "Going forward, we expect to make sizeable capex investments over the next several quarters to prepare for increased datacenter product production in 2025. We believe our US-based production ability, automated manufacturing and extensive experience uniquely position us to meet our customer's needs."

Full-year 2024 revenue of [$249.4 million](https://investors.ao-inc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/applied-optoelectronics-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-5) against $217.6 million in 2023 was a 14.6% improvement — meaningful, but not sufficient on its own to explain the stock rerating already underway. The market was pricing a dual-cycle thesis, not the trailing twelve months.

## Holding the base: Q1 and Q2 2025

Q1 2025 delivered $99.9 million — effectively flat with Q4 2024, but running at more than double the $40.7 million registered in Q1 2024. CATV set what was then a company revenue record for the quarter. In the datacenter segment, management disclosed something that would prove significant in hindsight: three new design wins with an existing hyperscale customer, alongside the first explicit public expression of confidence in a second-half 800G ramp.

> "We have seen and expect to continue to see a growing demand for our 400G and 800G products and we are actively working to build out our capacity to address this demand. Based on forecasts we are seeing, we have increased confidence in a second half of 2025 ramp in 800G sales." — Dr. Thompson Lin, [Q1 2025 earnings press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000168316825003290/aaoi_ex9901.htm), May 8, 2025

Q2 2025 added $103.0 million — a 3.1% sequential increase — but delivered a milestone in the 800G qualification sequence that the market had been watching closely. Management reported that AAOI's Taiwan facility had received approval from a major hyperscale customer for 800G product production. Dr. Lin's framing was careful about the remaining distance:

> "We made positive steps forward in our 800G qualification efforts following the approval of our Taiwan factory for 800G product production from one of our major hyperscale customers. We're approaching what we believe are the final stages for securing 800G product qualification and continue to believe that we will produce meaningful shipments of 800G products sometime in the second half of 2025." — Dr. Thompson Lin, [Q2 2025 earnings press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000168316825005755/aaoi_ex9901.htm), August 7, 2025

GAAP gross margin in Q2 2025 held at 30.3%, essentially equal to the 30.6% posted in Q1 2025. Two quarters together put $202.9 million on the top line in the first half of 2025, more than double the $84.0 million produced in the equivalent 2024 period. The cost structure was absorbing the volumes without margin deterioration.

## The dual-cycle pivot: Q3 2025

The quarter that crystallised the dual-cycle story most legibly was Q3 2025. Revenue of $118.6 million — a 15.1% sequential increase — was another record, but the composition was where the analytical weight sat.

CATV delivered $70.6 million, the highest single-quarter CATV result in AAOI's history, driven by 1.8 GHz amplifier shipments through Digicomm and, notably, by momentum with new CATV customers beyond the primary channel. Datacenter contributed $43.9 million, a figure that came in slightly below internal expectations; within the datacenter mix, 400G product revenues had contracted sharply year-on-year as that generation aged toward obsolescence, while the 800G qualification process moved into its stated final stages.

Lin's Q3 prepared remarks were the clearest articulation to date of AAOI's dual-engine positioning:

> "We continued to see strong demand in our CATV business, driven by the continued ramp in orders for our 1.8 GHz amplifier products. We believe that the appeal of our amplifiers and QuantumLink™ software is broad-based, which was evident by the continued momentum we saw with our largest customer as well as new customers during the quarter, and which led to the highest quarterly CATV revenue in our Company's history. We continued to make progress on securing 800G product qualification. We are nearing what we believe are the final stages of 800G product qualification with several customers, and we continue to believe that we will produce meaningful shipments of 800G products in the fourth quarter." — Dr. Thompson Lin, [Q3 2025 earnings press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000168316825008029/aaoi_ex9901.htm), November 6, 2025

Murry attributed the datacenter shortfall to logistics rather than demand, a distinction the market absorbed as constructive: "Exceptionally strong demand in our CATV business more than offset our datacenter revenue, which came in a touch below our expectations, largely due to the timing of certain shipments at quarter end due to various shipping and receiving delays." He also disclosed the forthcoming capacity exit rate — approximately 100,000 units per month of 800G production, with roughly 35% from the Sugar Land facility — a figure that would become directly relevant to domestic-supply-chain discussions in the following year.

## The crossover quarter: Q4 2025

Q4 2025 produced $134.3 million in revenue and the structural landmark that closed the dual-cycle narrative. Datacenter revenue of $74.9 million exceeded CATV revenue of $54.0 million within a single quarter — the first such inversion in company history, confirming that the mix was completing its rotation back toward AI infrastructure end-markets.

The full-year result was correspondingly transformative. FY2025 revenue of [$455.7 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000168316826001315/aaoi_ex9901.htm) against $249.4 million in FY2024 represented 82.8% growth. GAAP gross margin recovered to 30.0% from 24.8%. Net loss narrowed to $38.2 million from $186.7 million — still a loss, still carrying $493.1 million of accumulated deficit, but moving in the direction that years of trough operation had made structurally implausible.

> "We are pleased to deliver record fourth quarter results that were in line with or better than our expectations, and which capped off the strongest year in our company's history. Our results were driven by broad-based demand in both our CATV and datacenter businesses. We have considerable momentum entering 2026, and we believe we are well positioned to accelerate our growth this year." — Dr. Thompson Lin, [Q4 2025 / FY2025 earnings press release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000168316826001315/aaoi_ex9901.htm), February 26, 2026

Murry, in the same release, signalled the capital cycle intensifying: "We made tangible progress during the quarter on expanding our manufacturing capacity, which is a critical step as we prepare for higher-volume production of our next generation datacenter products. We believe we are well positioned for sustained growth and the capital investments underway are expected to fundamentally strengthen the company as we execute on the strong demand we see."

## The order book arrives

The FY2025 print closed one chapter; the announcements that followed within weeks opened the next. Between late March and early April 2026 — five weeks after the February 26 earnings release — AAOI announced a sequence of orders from a single major hyperscale customer totalling more than $324 million: $53 million for 800G transceivers, then more than $200 million for first-volume 1.6 terabit products, then an additional $71 million for 800G units. The customer was not named in the releases, but the market read the announcements in the context of the March 2025 Amazon warrant — a stock purchase right for up to 7.945 million shares vesting against volume purchase thresholds — issued as part of a hyperscale supply relationship.

The 1.6T component of that order was the more consequential element. It positioned AAOI as one of a small number of optical transceiver suppliers with qualified product above the 800G threshold — a generation that the broader industry expects to dominate AI datacenter interconnects through 2027. The Q1 2026 guidance issued with the May 7, 2026 earnings report — revenue of $150 million to $165 million — implied a quarterly run rate that had already exceeded the FY2025 annualised figure.

## How the market priced it

| Quarter | Revenue | Sequential Δ | Margin (GAAP) |
|---------|---------|-------------|----------------|
| Q3 2024 | $65.2M | — (trough) | 24.4% |
| Q4 2024 | $100.3M | +$35.1M (+53.8%) | 28.7% |
| Q1 2025 | $99.9M | –$0.4M (flat) | 30.6% |
| Q2 2025 | $103.0M | +$3.1M (+3.1%) | 30.3% |
| Q3 2025 | $118.6M | +$15.6M (+15.1%) | 28.0% |
| Q4 2025 | $134.3M | +$15.7M (+13.2%) | 31.2% |

The stock did not wait for the reported numbers. From the $1.50 trough, shares moved steadily through 2024 and the first half of 2025 as investors priced the dual-cycle thesis ahead of the revenue confirmation — trading well into double figures before the 800G qualification was formally announced. The FY2025 print in February 2026, combined with the March-April order book, extended the run to a five-year high of $223.10 before settling near $181 at the May 23, 2026 snapshot. A stock that had declined more than 98% from its prior peak had, in the space of roughly thirty months of reported sequential growth, retraced to within striking distance of that prior high in absolute share-price terms — even as the share count had expanded materially through the trough years' equity raises.

What the six-quarter sequence does not yet show is a GAAP-profitable company. The $493.1 million accumulated deficit remains on the balance sheet. Digicomm at 53.1% of FY2025 revenue and Microsoft at 28.8% constitute a concentration exposure that few institutional investors would regard as comfortable regardless of the order backlog. The sequential growth answered the recovery question convincingly. Whether the Amazon order book represents a genuine third revenue pillar — capable of diversifying concentration while sustaining the product-generation premium as 1.6T volumes scale — is the question FY2026 will answer.

chapters.title: The founder, his board, and the people who built the vertical stack
chapters.body:
## The founder who never left the lab

Thompson Lin did not set out to build a publicly traded datacenter supplier. He set out to solve a materials problem.

When Lin co-founded Applied Optoelectronics on 28 February 1997, he was still listed as a Senior Research Scientist at the University of Houston, where he had worked since 1994, and would remain, in the title of Research Associate Professor, until 2000. His doctorate from the University of Missouri-Columbia was in electrical and computer engineering; his undergraduate degree, from National Tsing Hua University in Taiwan, was in nuclear engineering. The combination — particle physics instincts grafted onto photonics — was not accidental. The InP compound semiconductors at the core of AAOI's vertical stack require the same tolerance for materials behaviour at the quantum level that nuclear engineering drills into its students. Lin never stopped being a working scientist. He simply acquired, over 28 years, a company to work through.

That unbroken tenure — Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer since inception — is without obvious parallel among US-listed optical components companies of comparable scale. He has held all three titles continuously as the company moved from Sugar Land startup to CATV supplier to near-bankrupt trough to AI-datacenter contender. Through the 2018-2023 period that accumulated roughly $493.1m in deficit on the balance sheet, Lin did not step aside. No separate president was installed. No activist-endorsed CEO transition was announced. The board's response to the trough was to back the founder's vertical-integration thesis and wait for the cycle to turn — which, in FY2025, it emphatically did, with revenue of $455.7m representing 82.8% year-on-year growth.

Lin's institutional affiliations reinforce the picture of a scientist-executive whose primary network is academic rather than financial. He joined the University of Missouri Chancellor's Advisory Group in May 2015 and chairs Missouri's Industrial Advisory Board for the College of Engineering, a role he has held since November 2016. These are not honorary sinecures. They are the kind of ongoing commitments that keep a founder connected to the basic-research pipeline from which the next generation of compound-semiconductor engineers will emerge — and from which AAOI has drawn talent for nearly three decades.

## One executive doing two jobs

The flatness of the senior-executive structure below Lin is striking for a company at AAOI's revenue scale. There is no Chief Operating Officer. The operational spine of North America and Asia is managed by two divisional general managers — Dr. Fred Chang as SVP and North America GM, and Shu-Hua (Joshua) Yeh as SVP and Asia GM — reporting, in practice, to a CEO who has never delegated the operating role to a layer between himself and his GMs.

Into that gap sits Stefan Murry, who holds the dual title of Chief Financial Officer and Chief Strategy Officer. The combined role is structurally significant and worth pausing on. In most companies at $450m-plus in annual revenue, the functions of financial planning and long-term strategy are kept separate to maintain an internal counterweight: the CFO models the numbers, the CSO or strategy head argues about what those numbers should be buying. At AAOI, both functions flow from one executive who is, by all observable evidence, closely aligned with the CEO's long-term thesis. The result is that capital allocation, investor communication, and product-roadmap prioritisation are integrated in a way that accelerates decision-making but compresses the internal debate that separate roles would generate. Whether that is a strength or a concentration risk depends on one's view of the thesis itself.

The rest of the named executive team carries a credential density unusual for a company of this size: three of the seven executives hold doctorates. Murry is Dr. Stefan Murry; Chang is Dr. Fred Chang; Klaus Alex Anselm, VP of Semiconductor Products, is Dr. Klaus Alex Anselm. The doctoral count matters because it signals where AAOI's competitive differentiation actually lives. This is not a company whose senior leadership was assembled to manage a distribution channel or optimise a sales-force structure. The people running the business are, in the main, the people who understand the physics of what the business makes. David Kuo, as SVP and Chief Legal and Compliance Officer, and Todd McCrum, as SVP and GM of the Broadband Access business unit, round out a team whose composition reflects a technologist-run operating company rather than a finance-led platform.

## The board that advises, not transforms

Seven directors sit on AAOI's board. Lin is Chairman. The six outside directors were not assembled to engineer a transaction or prepare for a relisting. They were assembled, over time, to govern a vertically-integrated semiconductor manufacturer run by a founder who does not intend to be replaced.

The most consequential outside director for understanding AAOI's institutional character is Richard B. Black, who chairs the Audit Committee. Black ran ECRM, Incorporated — a laser-based imaging equipment company — as CEO and Chairman from 1983 until its sale to Eastman Kodak in 2021: 38 years in the same chair at a laser company, which is itself a form of founder-CEO credibility. He has chaired the audit committee at two other public optical and photonics companies — GSI Group (where he also served as board chairman from 2006 to 2012) and Alliance Fiber Optics Products — and has been a director at TREX Enterprises since 2000. His formal pedigree includes a BS in Engineering from Texas A&M, an MBA from Harvard, and an honorary doctorate from Beloit College. Since 1990 he has served as a trustee of the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton, where he was vice chairman from 2006 to 2012 and has held trustee-emeritus status since. He also holds trustee roles at the American Indian College Fund, Beloit College, and Bard College, and sits on the Board of Governors of the University of Chicago's Smart Museum of Art. The breadth of that institutional portfolio places Black in the senior tier of the US technology-business establishment — the kind of figure who brings not just domain knowledge but the reputational anchoring that validates a small-cap's governance to institutional investors. For AAOI specifically, his 38 years in laser imaging and his audit-committee experience at GSI Group and Alliance Fiber Optics Products mean the person reviewing AAOI's financial controls genuinely understands what the company's factories are doing.

Che-Wei Lin — no relation to the CEO — represents the company's other axis: the Asia semiconductor supply chain that AAOI's Taipei and Ningbo operations are embedded in. He has been President of ASMedia Technology, a Taiwan-listed chipset maker majority-owned by ASUSTek, since November 2007, and Corporate VP of ASUSTek's Motherboard Business Unit since November 2009. Before that, 14 years at VIA Technologies, ending as President of the Desktop Platform Business Unit. He holds a BS in Electrical Engineering from Fu Jen University in Taiwan and an MS in Electrical Engineering from the University of Missouri. That Missouri connection — the same institution where Thompson Lin earned his MS and PhD — is the kind of personal-network detail that explains long board tenures in Asia-headquartered semiconductor companies. University networks in the Taiwan-US engineering diaspora function as persistent relationship infrastructure, and the Missouri link between the CEO and a sitting board member is almost certainly not coincidental.

Dr. Min-Chu (Mike) Chen chairs the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee and sits on the Audit Committee. A partner and board member at EverRich Capital since 2001, Chen served on the PCTEL board from March 1994 to June 2022 — a 28-year tenure that is its own statement about the board-governance philosophy he brings to AAOI. His PhD is in Ocean Engineering from Oregon State University; his operating background spans Exxon, Transocean, petrochemical-equipment management through C&C International Services, and a co-founder role at EABO Information Technology in Shanghai, an IIoT company. The cross-industrial profile is unusual for an optics-company board but consistent with the reality of AAOI's Asia manufacturing footprint: governing a company with 2,881 employees in China and 1,262 in Taiwan requires directors who understand cross-border industrial operations, not just semiconductor product cycles.

William H. Yeh chairs the Compensation Committee and is the board member who most clearly represents AAOI's Sugar Land geographic roots. As CEO and President of Golden Star Management — a real-estate investment and management company he has run since 1997 — and as Vice Chairman of Central Bancorp from 1997 to 2014 (and subsequent advisor to Hanmi Bank for Texas), Yeh is a Texas/Taiwan-bridge community-banking and real-estate executive. His BS is from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan; his MS from the University of Houston-Clear Lake. Those Houston-area institutional relationships, built over nearly three decades, are part of the fabric that has kept AAOI anchored in Sugar Land rather than relocating to a semiconductor cluster with lower real-estate costs.

Dr. Elizabeth Loboa brings the board's only explicitly academic-research-administration voice. Since 2020 she has served as Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs at Southern Methodist University. Before that, from 2018 to 2020, she was Vice Chancellor for Strategic Partnerships and Dean at the University of Missouri — a tenure that overlaps directly with Thompson Lin's continuing role on Missouri's Chancellor's Advisory Group. Her Stanford PhD in mechanical engineering and UC Davis undergraduate degree mark her as a research-intensive university administrator rather than an industry operator, and she is the board member most clearly outside AAOI's operating ecosystem. That independence, combined with her governance committee role, is precisely the function she serves.

Cynthia (Cindy) DeLaney rounds out the Audit Committee with a profile that is rarer on semi-company boards than it might appear: a practising commodity-markets professional with an engineering undergraduate degree. She began her career as an electrical engineer at Arco Chemical in 1991, moved into MTBE and gasoline-component trading at Arco and Koch, and has been Global Fuel Oil commodity trading manager at Shell Trading since January 2014 and a director and vice president of Shell Trading US Company since October 2016. Shell's US trading operations are Houston-based. The geographic bond to Sugar Land is direct, and her commodity-risk and mark-to-market experience brings to the Audit Committee a literacy in complex financial instruments that is directly relevant as AAOI's customer concentration and large forward-order dynamics create new balance-sheet exposures.

## What the composition says

Taken together, the board is unusually substantive for a sub-$1bn small-cap operating in optical and photonics. Three directors — Black in laser imaging, Che-Wei Lin in Asia semiconductor chipsets, and DeLaney in engineering and commodity markets — carry deep technical and operating experience in adjacent industries. Loboa brings academic-research rigour and institutional independence. Chen brings cross-border industrial and governance experience. Yeh brings the community-banking and real-estate network stability that has underpinned the company's Texas base.

What the board does not contain is equally telling. There is no former Citi CFO, no ex-Deutsche Bank head of corporate finance, no private-equity partner brought in to engineer a value-creation event. The contrast with the boards that typically accompany a near-US-listing or pre-acquisition transformation — the kind of board Sivers Semiconductors assembled ahead of its Nasdaq ambitions, for instance — is explicit. AAOI's board is configured to advise and audit a founder-CEO who has run the company for 28 years and intends to continue running it. That difference is not incidental to the equity story. It is the equity story: the upside, if the AI-datacenter ramp sustains, accrues to a structure that Thompson Lin built and still controls. The board is there to make sure he keeps building it responsibly, not to replace him or sell the company out from under him.

chapters.title: Two customers, three factories, one warrant
chapters.body:
## The arithmetic of dependence

Two names accounted for 81.9 cents of every dollar Applied Optoelectronics collected in fiscal 2025: Digicomm International at 53.1% and Microsoft at 28.8%, together representing roughly $373 million of the company's record $455.7 million in revenue. That ratio, disclosed in the [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001158114/000143774926005875/aaoi20251231_10k.htm), would be alarming for a mature industrial manufacturer. For a company mid-acceleration through the most consequential infrastructure cycle in a decade, it reads differently — as the tax on being early.

The three-year trajectory tells the underlying story:

| Customer | FY2023 share | FY2024 share | FY2025 share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Digicomm International | 11.3% | 34.1% | 53.1% |
| Microsoft | 46.6% | 43.7% | 28.8% |
| Combined | 57.9% | 77.8% | 81.9% |

The surface reading is divergence — Digicomm tripling while Microsoft fades. The underlying reality is that both relationships are growing in absolute dollars; the mix is simply being pulled by which growth is faster. AAOI's total revenue rose 82.8% year-over-year in 2025, from $249.4 million to $455.7 million. Microsoft's declining percentage share nonetheless corresponded to an estimated $131 million in recognised revenue — more in absolute terms than it generated in earlier years when its share looked larger against a smaller denominator.

## Digicomm and the DOCSIS cycle

Digicomm International is not a name that appears in datacenter infrastructure discussions. It is a privately-held US distributor of broadband network equipment, acquired by The Beekman Group in 2018, and its business is almost entirely upstream of the AI compute buildout. What Digicomm sells — and what drove its revenue share at AAOI from 11.3% to 53.1% in two years — is the cable industry's response to fibre overbuilders.

Comcast, Charter, Cox, and the other Tier-1 multiple system operators face competitive pressure from telco fibre that their existing hybrid fibre-coaxial plants were not designed to match. The answer the industry settled on was DOCSIS 4.0, which requires plant upgrades to support 1.8 GHz transmission — roughly double the upper frequency bound of the previous DOCSIS 3.1 infrastructure. AAOI's HFC amplifier lineup, including the Quantum18 and QuantumLink products, is purpose-built for that upgrade cycle. Digicomm is the channel through which those amplifiers reach the MSO plant operators.

The result is a revenue line that looks, from the outside, like extraordinary customer concentration but is, in substance, a concentrated channel to a fragmented end-market of cable operators. Digicomm does not consume the product; it distributes it. The underlying demand is diffused across the North American cable plant. Whether that distinction matters for continuity-of-revenue purposes depends on whether DOCSIS 4.0 capital expenditure remains a cable-industry priority — a question that reaches beyond AAOI's control and into the capex disciplines of companies like Comcast and Charter.

## Microsoft and the 800G inflection

Microsoft's position in AAOI's revenue mix is structurally different from Digicomm's. It is a direct hyperscale datacenter customer with a years-long qualified relationship, and it is the commercial reason AAOI crossed the 30.0% GAAP gross margin threshold in FY2025, up from 24.8% the prior year. The causal link is product mix: Microsoft has been the primary customer for AAOI's 800G OSFP DR8 transceivers, and the economics of 800G are meaningfully better than the 400G products that defined the prior cycle.

The qualification process for a new transceiver generation at a hyperscaler of Microsoft's scale is not trivial. It requires months of interoperability testing and field validation before volume purchase orders flow.
